title: Centralized Lakehouse or Domain-Owned Mesh?
purpose: Decide whether a Fabric estate should stay one centrally-owned lakehouse or split into Fabric domains with domain-owned workspaces, based on team autonomy, governance maturity, platform capacity, and cross-domain consumption needs.
accessibleSummary: A decision tree with a root question about team autonomy and ownership pressure. If one central team can own all data products, the tree recommends a centralized lakehouse. If multiple business areas need to own their own data products, it branches into a domain-owned model, then asks whether tenant governance is mature enough to delegate; if not, it warns against delegating before standards exist. It then asks whether capacity should be split per domain, and finally shows cross-domain consumption resolving through OneLake shortcuts rather than data copies.
longDescription: This is a decision tree, not a pipeline. The root question is whether ownership pressure genuinely exists: many independent business areas each wanting to define and evolve their own data products. If not, a single centralized lakehouse under one team is simpler and is the recommended default. If ownership pressure is real, the tree moves to a domain-owned model built from Fabric domains grouping workspaces by business area, but gates that move on governance maturity — delegating tenant-wide policy to domains before standards exist is a documented anti-pattern this diagram calls out as a warning. Assuming governance is ready, the tree asks whether capacity should be split per domain, using capacity as the isolation and chargeback boundary that throttles independently. It closes on how domains consume each other's data without copying: OneLake shortcuts, which read producer-owned data in place under the calling user's identity, keeping the mesh model on Fabric's single tenant-wide OneLake rather than one physical lake per domain — the exact antipattern OneLake was built to eliminate.

nodes.label: Does real ownership pressure exist?
nodes.summary: Root question: do multiple business areas need to own their own data products, or can one team own it all?
nodes.detail: Data mesh is an operating model, not a Fabric feature or a product recommendation — this decision is an architectural interpretation, not a sourced platform guarantee. The first question is whether the organization has multiple business areas that genuinely need to define, evolve, and be accountable for their own data products, or whether one central team can realistically own everything without becoming a bottleneck.
nodes.whyItMatters: Splitting into domains before ownership pressure is real adds coordination overhead — separate workspaces, separate governance delegation, separate capacity planning — for a problem that doesn't yet exist. This question exists to stop premature mesh adoption.

inputs: Number of business areas producing or needing to own analytical data
Whether a central team is currently a bottleneck for new data products
Organizational appetite for federated ownership vs central control
processing: Count genuinely independent business data owners (not just consumers)
Assess whether the central team's backlog is the limiting factor for new data products
Weigh coordination cost of a mesh model against the cost of continued centralization
outputs: A routed decision: stay centralized, or move to a domain-owned model
drill.example: A single finance team currently owns all reporting data for a 200-person company with one business line; there's no second business area demanding ownership, so centralized stays the right answer despite the term 'data mesh' being popular in industry reading.
controls: Write down which business areas are asking for ownership, not just which teams consume data
failureModes: Adopting domain terminology and structure because it's fashionable, not because ownership pressure is real
Underestimating a genuine cross-team ownership conflict and staying centralized past the point it still works

nodes.label: Centralized lakehouse, one team
nodes.summary: One team owns one lakehouse and its workspaces; simplest governance, single point of accountability.
nodes.detail: A single central team owns the lakehouse, its workspaces, and its data products. OneLake is already tenant-wide and single, so this is the default topology Fabric provisions with no domain structure layered on top — one team, one set of governance settings, one capacity strategy.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the right answer far more often than mesh advocacy suggests. It has none of the delegation, standards, and cross-domain-consumption overhead the rest of this tree exists to manage.

inputs: A single business's data products and reporting needs
processing: Provision one or a small number of workspaces under one team
Apply tenant-wide governance settings directly with no domain delegation layer
Assign one capacity or a small, simply-managed set
outputs: A lakehouse estate with one clear owner and minimal coordination overhead
drill.example: A single analytics team owns the lakehouse workspace, curates the medallion layers, and publishes the semantic model directly — no domain admin layer, no cross-domain shortcut consumption to reason about.
controls: Revisit this decision if a second business area starts demanding its own data-product ownership
failureModes: Staying centralized long after a second team's ownership demands make the central team an actual bottleneck
Mistaking simple team size for architectural necessity and never revisiting the decision

nodes.label: Fabric domains group workspaces
nodes.summary: Domains group workspaces by business area, giving a delegation point above the workspace.
nodes.detail: A Fabric domain groups workspaces into a logical business area (Finance, Marketing, and so on), giving administrators a level above the individual workspace at which to delegate management and apply governance policies. Domains can contain subdomains, and workspace content can be filtered by domain in the OneLake catalog.
nodes.whyItMatters: Domains are the concrete Fabric construct that makes a mesh operating model implementable at all — without them, 'domain ownership' would have no platform boundary to attach to, only a policy document.

evidence.note: Domains let an organization group workspaces into logical business areas (for example Finance or Marketing), giving administrators a level above the workspace at which to delegate management and apply governance policies.

Domains let organizations logically group Fabric content by business area, enabling each department to apply its own governance settings where those settings have been delegated from the tenant level; domains can contain subdomains, and workspace content can be filtered by domain in the OneLake catalog.

inputs: Business-area boundaries identified in the ownership question
processing: Create a domain per genuine business-area owner
Assign the relevant workspaces to each domain
Delegate domain-level governance settings from the tenant admin
outputs: A domain layer above workspaces, filterable in the OneLake catalog
A named point of delegated authority per business area
drill.example: A retailer creates Merchandising and Logistics domains, each grouping the workspaces that team already owns, so the OneLake catalog can be filtered to 'show me only Merchandising's endorsed data products.'
controls: Which governance settings are delegated to domain admins vs kept tenant-wide
Whether subdomains are needed for a business area with its own sub-teams
failureModes: Creating domains that don't map to any real ownership boundary, adding structure with no delegation benefit
Leaving domains empty of delegated authority, so they're organizational labels rather than functioning governance boundaries

nodes.label: Is tenant governance mature enough to delegate?
nodes.summary: Gate: domains only work if tenant-wide standards already exist to delegate from.
nodes.detail: Fabric's governance model is a three-tier hierarchy — tenant-wide defaults, domain-level overrides for delegated settings, and workspace-level controls — where domain admins can only override settings the tenant has explicitly delegated to them. This question checks whether that tenant-wide baseline (sensitivity labels, endorsement policy, baseline controls) is mature enough to delegate from before domains are stood up.
nodes.whyItMatters: Delegating governance authority to domains before tenant-wide standards exist doesn't create autonomy — it creates inconsistency, because each domain invents its own rules with nothing to delegate from.

inputs: Existing tenant-wide sensitivity-label policy, endorsement process, and baseline controls (or their absence)
processing: Audit whether tenant-wide governance defaults are actually defined and enforced today
Identify which specific settings are safe to delegate to domain admins vs must stay tenant-wide
Only proceed to domain delegation once this baseline exists
outputs: A go/no-go on domain governance delegation, and an explicit list of what's delegated vs tenant-wide
drill.example: A tenant with no defined sensitivity-label taxonomy or endorsement process stands up five domains anyway; each domain admin invents their own labeling convention, and cross-domain data products become impossible to reason about consistently.
controls: Define tenant-wide governance standards before delegating any of them to domains
Keep a written list of exactly which settings each domain is allowed to override
failureModes: Standing up domains before any tenant-wide governance baseline exists — the trap this diagram flags explicitly
Delegating too much too fast, so domains diverge on labeling, endorsement, and access policy in ways that break cross-domain trust

nodes.label: Trap: domains without governance baseline
nodes.summary: Delegating governance authority before tenant standards exist produces inconsistent, untrustworthy domains.
nodes.detail: If domains are created and governance delegated before tenant-wide sensitivity-label policy, endorsement standards, and baseline controls are defined, each domain ends up inventing its own conventions independently. The result looks like domain autonomy but is actually governance fragmentation — cross-domain consumers can no longer trust that a 'Certified' label or a sensitivity classification means the same thing in two different domains.
nodes.whyItMatters: This failure mode is easy to miss because it looks like the mesh model working as intended — domains making their own decisions. The damage only becomes visible when a consumer in one domain misinterprets another domain's data because the same-looking governance signal means something different there.

inputs: Domains created without a delegated tenant-wide governance baseline
processing: Each domain admin independently decides labeling, endorsement, and access conventions
No tenant-level standard exists to reconcile the divergence
Cross-domain consumers hit inconsistent signals without warning
outputs: Fragmented, untrustworthy governance signals across domains that undermine the catalog's discoverability promise
drill.example: Domain A marks anything reviewed by a manager as 'Certified'; Domain B reserves 'Certified' for data with automated quality tests. A consumer trusts a Certified label from Domain B's rigor and applies the same trust to Domain A's data, which was held to a much lower bar.
controls: Freeze domain creation until tenant-wide endorsement and labeling standards are published
Audit domain governance settings periodically against the tenant baseline for drift
failureModes: Silent trust erosion — nobody notices until a bad decision is traced back to a misread governance signal
Retrofitting standards after domains are already diverged, which is far more disruptive than defining them first

nodes.label: Split capacity per domain?
nodes.summary: Decide whether each domain gets its own capacity for isolation and chargeback, or shares one.
nodes.detail: Because Fabric enforces throttling at the capacity level rather than the tenant level, a saturated capacity only affects the workspaces assigned to it. Splitting capacities per domain (or per environment stage) gives workload isolation and cost attribution — a noisy domain's throttling doesn't spill into another domain's capacity.
nodes.whyItMatters: Capacity is the only isolation boundary in this whole model that actually stops one domain's workload from degrading another's performance — governance and workspace boundaries don't provide that.

evidence.note: Fabric enforces throttling at the capacity level rather than the tenant level, so a saturated capacity only affects the workspaces assigned to it; other capacities continue operating normally.

Capacities serve as isolation boundaries for compute resources and chargebacks, and the recommended practice is to split capacities by environment stage to achieve workload isolation and cost attribution.

inputs: Each domain's expected workload volume and criticality
processing: Assign each domain's workspaces to its own capacity where isolation or chargeback matters
Share a single capacity across low-volume domains where isolation isn't worth the overhead
Monitor per-capacity throttling independently per domain
outputs: A capacity assignment map: dedicated capacities for domains needing isolation, shared capacity for the rest
drill.example: The Merchandising domain gets its own F64 capacity because its nightly batch jobs are heavy and unpredictable, while three small back-office domains share one smaller capacity since none of them individually justifies dedicated compute.
controls: Capacity SKU sizing per domain's actual workload, not a uniform default
Periodic review of whether a shared capacity's noisy-neighbor risk has grown past acceptable
failureModes: Over-splitting capacities for domains too small to justify dedicated compute, inflating cost with no isolation benefit
Under-splitting, so one domain's throttling silently degrades every domain sharing its capacity

nodes.label: Cross-domain reads via OneLake shortcuts
nodes.summary: Consuming domains read producer-owned data in place through shortcuts, never by copying it.
nodes.detail: A OneLake shortcut is an embedded reference that points at another location, giving a consuming domain access to a producing domain's data without copying it or building an ETL pipeline. Internal shortcuts authorize access with the calling user's own identity, which must hold read permission at the target — the producing domain stays the source of truth.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is what keeps the mesh model from degenerating into per-domain data lakes with duplicated copies — the exact pre-OneLake antipattern the platform was built to eliminate. Ownership stays with the producer; consumption happens in place.

evidence.note: A shortcut is an embedded reference inside OneLake that points at another file-store location, giving workloads access to external operational data without copying it or building ETL pipelines.

Internal OneLake shortcuts can target data in other Fabric items across items and workspaces, and access through them is authorized with the calling user's own identity, which must hold read permission at the target.

Standing up separate physical data lakes per business group, a common pre-OneLake practice, is an antipattern in Fabric because it recreates resource-management overhead and data duplication that the single tenant-wide OneLake with workspaces and shortcuts is designed to eliminate.

inputs: An endorsed, published data product in a producing domain's workspace
processing: Consuming domain creates a OneLake shortcut targeting the producer's table
Access is authorized under the calling user's own identity against the producer's permissions
Consumer queries the shortcut as if it were a local table, with no data movement
outputs: Live, governed, zero-copy access to another domain's data product
drill.example: The Finance domain shortcuts into Merchandising's gold sales table to build a cross-domain profitability report, reading Merchandising's live data under the report author's own OneLake read permissions rather than requesting an export.
controls: Grant read permission at the target scoped to what the consuming domain actually needs
Endorse/certify the producer table so consumers know it's a trustworthy data product before shortcutting to it
failureModes: A consuming domain bypassing shortcuts and requesting a data copy 'to be safe', reintroducing duplication and staleness
Producer renaming or moving the shortcut target, breaking every consuming domain's shortcut with no warning

edges.label: one team can own it all
tenant baseline exists, safe to delegate

walkthrough.title: 1. Is ownership pressure real?
walkthrough.explanation: Before adopting any mesh terminology, check whether multiple business areas genuinely need to own their own data products, or whether one team can still do it all.

walkthrough.title: 2a. Stay centralized if pressure isn't real
walkthrough.explanation: The simplest, most common right answer: one team, one lakehouse, no domain delegation overhead.

walkthrough.title: 2b. Domains are the Fabric construct for mesh
walkthrough.explanation: If ownership pressure is real, Fabric domains group workspaces by business area and give a level above the workspace to delegate governance.

walkthrough.title: 3. Gate: is governance ready to delegate?
walkthrough.explanation: Domains only work if there's a tenant-wide baseline to delegate from — this question stops premature delegation before it happens.

walkthrough.title: 4. Warning: delegating too early fragments governance
walkthrough.explanation: Standing up domains before tenant standards exist looks like autonomy but produces inconsistent, untrustworthy governance signals across domains.

walkthrough.title: 5. Split capacity for isolation and chargeback
walkthrough.explanation: Once governance is ready, decide which domains need dedicated capacity — the actual boundary that stops one domain's throttling from degrading another's.

walkthrough.title: 6. Consume across domains via shortcuts, not copies
walkthrough.explanation: The tree closes on how domains read each other's data: OneLake shortcuts, live and in place, keeping the tenant on one OneLake instead of fragmenting into per-domain lakes.
